content.p: Raja Raghuvanshi, a 28-year-old transport businessman from Indore in Madhya Pradesh, married Sonam Raghuvanshi in May 2025 and took her to Meghalaya for their honeymoon. On 23 May the couple disappeared in the hills around Sohra, also known as Cherrapunji. Ten days later searchers found his body at the bottom of a gorge near Wei Sawdong Falls. His wife was missing for nearly a week longer. When she was found, in Uttar Pradesh, the police accused her of arranging the killing.

Meghalaya Police allege that Sonam Raghuvanshi plotted the murder with a man they describe as her lover, Raj Kushwaha, and that three men from Madhya Pradesh carried it out in her presence. All five have pleaded not guilty, and Sonam Raghuvanshi says she has been falsely implicated. The case, which the Indian press calls the "honeymoon murder", is on trial in Shillong. The dispute that has gone furthest so far, all the way to the Supreme Court, was a procedural one: whether a section number typed wrongly on her arrest papers was enough to set her free.

Most reports date the wedding to 11 May 2025; the Meghalaya High Court reports in India Legal and LawBeat give 12 May. Sonam Raghuvanshi was 24, according to Arunachal24. The couple left Indore for the north-east on 20 May, and a police press release says they came to Shillong on 21 May before going on to Sohra, a popular tourist destination.

On 22 May, according to ETV Bharat, they rode a rented scooter to the village of Mawlakhiat, above Nongriat and its double-decker living root bridge. They stayed at a homestay in Nongriat and checked out on 23 May, the day Raja Raghuvanshi was last seen alive.

The families in Indore lost contact with the couple. The rented scooter was found abandoned, but the reports disagree about where and when: ETV Bharat said it was found on 24 May outside a cafe on the road from Shillong to Sohra, Arunachal24 placed it in Sohrarim, and a timeline published by The Bridge Chronicle gave 31 May and a spot near a roadside eatery. The police say the couple was reported missing on 26 May, and a large search began.

It ran for a week across difficult ground. Sohra police were joined by a police special operations team, the national and state disaster response forces, trekking groups and people from the surrounding villages, and drones were used. Both families pressed for a central investigation. Madhya Pradesh Chief Minister Mohan Yadav said he had asked the Union Home Minister, Amit Shah, to order an inquiry by the Central Bureau of Investigation. Sonam Raghuvanshi's father, Devi Singh Raghuvanshi, accused the Meghalaya Police of negligence and insisted his daughter had been kidnapped. "My daughter has been abducted and is still in the clutches of her captors," he said.

On 2 June the searchers found Raja Raghuvanshi's decomposed body in a deep gorge at Arliang Riat Kunongrim, Umblai, below the parking area at Wei Sawdong. His brother identified him by a tattoo. A gold ring and a neck chain were missing. Highland Post reported that the body had two sharp cuts to the head, and the post-mortem recorded head injuries from a sharp weapon. A bloodstained machete was recovered near the gorge the next day, along with a white shirt and a smartwatch, and later a raincoat resembling one the couple had used turned up in the village of Mawkma, roughly halfway between Sohrarim and the gorge. The missing-person case became a murder inquiry. Vipin Raghuvanshi, the victim's elder brother, filed the formal complaint at Sohra police station on 3 June, and a special investigation team was set up under a superintendent of police with four deputies.

The first public sign that the couple had not been alone came from Albert Pde, a tourist guide in Mawlakhiat. He had offered his services to the couple on 22 May, but they turned him down and hired someone else. He told reporters that at about 10 a.m. on 23 May he saw the two of them climbing the more than 3,000 steps from Nongriat back up to Mawlakhiat in the company of three men. The men were speaking Hindi, he said, so he took them for outsiders. The police later listed the guide among the witnesses who saw the accused together.

On 9 June the Director General of Meghalaya Police, Idashisha Nongrang, announced a breakthrough. Sonam Raghuvanshi had been found in Ghazipur district, Uttar Pradesh, near a roadside eatery on the Varanasi-Ghazipur highway, after contacting her family. "Sonam surrendered at the Nandganj police station in UP, and was subsequently arrested," Nongrang said. In overnight raids the special investigation team picked up one man in Uttar Pradesh and two in Indore, and Nongrang said the men had told investigators that the wife had hired them to kill her husband. Meghalaya Chief Minister Conrad K. Sangma praised the force for a "major breakthrough" within seven days. The remaining suspect was caught within days; The Bridge Chronicle dated the five arrests to 8 to 11 June.

Whether she gave herself up is still disputed. The police and the state government call it a surrender. Her lawyer told the Supreme Court in 2026 that she was arrested in Ghazipur and that the arrest was being misrepresented. Her father rejected the accusation outright. "My daughter is innocent," he said, adding that the marriage had the consent of both families.

According to the police she did not go straight to Uttar Pradesh but hid after the killing in a building in Indore. ETV Bharat later reported that a driver, Pradeep Sahu, who testified by video link from Indore, took her from there on to Ghazipur. In late June police arrested three more men in Madhya Pradesh on charges of destroying or hiding evidence: Silome James, described by Highland Post as a property dealer; Lokendra Singh Tomar, the owner of the building; and a security guard named in reports as Balbir, Balveer or Balla Ahirwar. All three were later released on bail.

On 5 September 2025, the date given by Highland Post and the court record (The Tribune reported it as 6 September), the special investigation team filed a charge sheet of 790 pages before the Judicial Magistrate First Class in Sohra. It accused Sonam Raghuvanshi, Raj Kushwaha, Vishal Singh Chauhan, Akash Singh Rajput and Anand Kurmi under the new criminal code, the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, of murder, causing evidence to disappear and criminal conspiracy. Kushwaha was 21, according to India Legal.

"It is conclusively (proven) that Smti Sonam Raja Raghuvanshi was in a relationship with Shri Raj Kushwaha and a criminal conspiracy was hatched by Raj Kushwaha along with Sonam and the three assailants to murder Raja Raghuvanshi under the pretext of a honeymoon to Sohra," Superintendent Vivek Syiem said. According to Syiem, as reported by The Bridge Chronicle, her family had disapproved of her relationship with Kushwaha and arranged the marriage to Raghuvanshi, and she had warned them of serious consequences if they went ahead. Other police statements described money as a motive, alleging that she conspired with the hired men for financial gain.

The police account of the killing itself is short. They say Chauhan, Rajput and Kurmi attacked Raghuvanshi at the Wei Sawdong spot with Sonam Raghuvanshi there; that Chauhan struck the first blow with a machete; and that she ran off when her husband began to bleed and cry out and returned only after he was dead. The body was thrown into the gorge. A second machete was found in the same gorge, and the white shirt recovered there was believed to be Rajput's. India TV reported that, according to the charge sheet, the plan failed several times and succeeded only at the fourth attempt, near the falls.

Police said the case rested on the recovered weapons, bloodstained clothing, CCTV footage of the couple, call records, travel and financial records, and the accounts of several witnesses. They also said the accused had confessed under interrogation, and took Sonam Raghuvanshi and three others back to Sohra to reconstruct the scene.

The killing also caused anger in Meghalaya. Tourism matters to Sohra, and residents and officials demanded apologies from the victim's family and from media outlets for coverage they said had damaged the state's name.

Charges were framed on 28 October 2025. The five accused, represented by legal aid counsel S. Rana and P. Pradhan, pleaded not guilty. According to the court record summarised by SCC Times, she was charged under four sections of the code: 103(1), the murder section, together with 238(a), 309(6) and 3(6). Evidence began on 11 November 2025 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Judicial) in Shillong, with Vipin Raghuvanshi as the first witness. His testimony ran out of time and was carried over to 26 November. The Special Public Prosecutor, K.C. Gautam, told reporters the case had about 90 witnesses. "I must say, it's a watertight chargesheet," he said.

Progress was slow. On 4 February 2026 the Shillong court acquitted Tomar and the watchman, ETV Bharat reported. Six days later the police filed a supplementary charge sheet that sought the discharge of the same two men, named Silome James as a co-accused, and added offences under the Arms Act against Sonam Raghuvanshi, Kushwaha and Chauhan. Her lawyers said the court would now have to revisit the charges, and that the trial had stood still since 3 February through no fault of hers. By the summer only four witnesses had testified.

Sonam Raghuvanshi had applied for bail three times and been refused each time. In her fourth application she argued for the first time that she had never been properly told why she was arrested, as Article 22(1) of the Constitution requires. The trial court agreed and granted her bail on 27 or 28 April 2026; reports differ on the date. The arrest memo, the checklist justifying the arrest, the intimation of her rights and the extract of the case diary all cited Section 403(1) of the code rather than Section 103(1), the murder section. The form headed "Intimation of Grounds of Arrest", handed to her at a centre in Ghazipur on 9 June 2025, was a template of about seventeen entries. None of its boxes was ticked, and it included irrelevant items such as desertion from the armed forces and an offence committed outside India. The court found that she had never been told in clear terms what she was accused of, and released her on a personal bond of 50,000 rupees with two sureties, on condition that she did not abscond, tamper with witnesses or leave the court's jurisdiction without permission.

Raj Kushwaha applied the next day. The court rejected his application without considering its merits, because he had not disclosed his earlier bail applications as the Supreme Court requires. In early May it refused bail to Kushwaha, Chauhan, Rajput and Kurmi, who had argued that they deserved the same treatment as her. Kushwaha's lawyer had argued that he was not at the scene and that no weapon was recovered from him.

The state asked the Meghalaya High Court to cancel her bail. Advocate General Amit Kumar argued that she had always known she was held for murder: she had signed the arrest papers, sat through repeated remand hearings with a lawyer, and filed three earlier bail applications. The 403 was a typing error, he said. Justice W. Diengdoh asked why the same typing error appeared in every document, and observed that the forms looked like templates filled in without thought. On 29 June 2026 he dismissed the state's petition, holding that the defect at the very start of the arrest could not be cured afterwards. He added that he was not passing judgment on the investigation, the charge sheet or the trial.

Meghalaya went to the Supreme Court, represented by Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, who argued that she was likely to abscond. On 3 July the court declined to suspend the High Court's order, while expressing reservations about it. At a hearing on 21 July the bench of Justices M.M. Sundresh and P.B. Varale put two options to her counsel: argue the case in full, or surrender while the public witnesses were examined. The bench also asked about her conduct after the killing and why she had not raised the arrest papers earlier. "The case of the prosecution is that you along with the deceased went to that place. That is the foundational fact," it said. In her written reply she maintained that she was innocent and that the case against her was built on circumstantial evidence.

On 23 July 2026 the court cancelled her bail. "It's not as if the respondent was not served with the grounds of arrest. There's a difference between non-service and giving adequate reasons thereunder," the bench said. In the second kind of case, it said, the accused must show prejudice, and should raise the point at the first opportunity. It held that both lower courts had erred, given the seriousness of the charge and her three earlier refusals, and that her continued release might hinder the trial now under way. Most reports said she was given three weeks to surrender, though The News Mill quoted the order as allowing two. If the trial has not ended within six months, she may apply again.

She surrendered to the trial court in Shillong at the end of July and was sent back to judicial custody after nearly three months on bail. Vipin Raghuvanshi welcomed the ruling and said he hoped everyone responsible for his brother's death would be punished severely. The family has continued to demand that the case be handed to the Central Bureau of Investigation. Vipin Raghuvanshi has said that if the central agency had investigated from the start, she would not have been able to exploit the legal lapses of the Meghalaya Police. In all, eight people were arrested in connection with the killing. None of the five main accused has been convicted, and the trial continues.
